paragraphs.text: 1.1. In Ephesus there lived a man among the foremost in power there, Lycomedes by name. To this Lycomedes was born, by a local woman named Themisto, a son, Habrocomes, a great marvel of beauty such as had never appeared before, either in Ionia or in any other land.

1.2. This Habrocomes grew daily more beautiful, and along with his bodily graces the goods of his soul flowered together with them. He cultivated every branch of learning and practised music of many kinds; hunting, riding, and fighting in armour were his accustomed exercises.

1.3. He was an object of devoted attention not only to all the Ephesians but also to the inhabitants of the rest of Asia, and they placed great hopes in him, that he would be a citizen of distinction. They treated the youth as a god, and there were already some who, on seeing him, bowed down and offered prayers.

1.4. The youth thought highly of himself, and prided himself on the achievements of his soul, but far more on the beauty of his body. He looked down on everything else that was called beautiful as inferior, and nothing seemed to him worthy of Habrocomes, no sight, no sound.

1.5. If he heard that some boy was handsome or some girl shapely, he laughed at those who said so, as not knowing that he alone was beautiful. Love he did not even consider to be a god, but cast him out altogether, accounting him as nothing, saying that no one would ever fall in love or submit to the god against his will.

1.6. If anywhere he saw a temple or a statue of Love, he laughed, and declared himself more beautiful than any Love. And so it was: for wherever Habrocomes was seen, no statue appeared beautiful and no painted image won praise.

2.1. At this Love grew angry, for the god is contentious and pitiless toward the proud. He sought some stratagem against the youth, who seemed hard for the god himself to capture. So he armed himself fully, took up all the power of his amorous charms, and marched against Habrocomes.

2.2. A local festival of Artemis was being celebrated, with a procession from the city to the temple, which is seven stades away. All the local maidens had to walk in procession richly adorned, and the young men of the same age as Habrocomes. He himself was about sixteen years old, was enrolled among the youths, and held the foremost place in the procession.

2.3. A great crowd had gathered for the spectacle, many of them townspeople and many strangers, for it was the custom at that festival for bridegrooms to be found for the maidens and wives for the young men.

2.4. The members of the procession passed by in file: first the sacred objects, torches, baskets, and incense; after these horses, dogs, and hunting gear, some of it for war but most for peace. And each of the maidens was adorned as if for a lover.

2.5. At the head of the line of maidens was Anthia, daughter of Megamedes and Euippe, of the local people. The beauty of Anthia was a thing to marvel at, and she far surpassed the other maidens. She was fourteen years old, her body was in the flower of its loveliness,

2.6. and the elegance of her bearing added much to her grace. Her hair was golden, mostly let loose, a little of it braided, and it stirred with the movement of the breezes; her eyes were lively, bright as a young girl's, yet stern as a chaste woman's; her tunic was deep purple, belted to the knee, falling to the elbows, a fawnskin wrapped about her, a quiver slung from her shoulder, a bow and javelins carried, and dogs following.

2.7. Often when they saw her at the precinct the Ephesians bowed down to her as to Artemis. And so on this occasion too, when she appeared, the crowd cried out, and the voices of the onlookers were of many kinds: some, in their astonishment, said she was the goddess; others, that she was someone else fashioned by the goddess in her likeness. But all prayed and bowed down and called her parents blessed; and Anthia the beautiful was on the lips of all who beheld her.

2.8. When the throng of maidens had passed by, no one spoke of anything but Anthia. But when Habrocomes appeared with the young men, then, though the spectacle of the maidens had been a fine one, everyone who saw Habrocomes forgot them and turned their gaze upon him, crying out, struck by the sight, "Beautiful Habrocomes!" and "such as no other, the very image of a beautiful god."

2.9. Some even added this: "What a marriage it would be between Habrocomes and Anthia!" And these were the first exercises of Love's art. Soon the report about each of them reached the other: Anthia longed to see Habrocomes, and Habrocomes, until then untouched by love, longed to see Anthia.

3.1. So when the procession was over, and the whole crowd had gone into the temple to sacrifice, and the order of the procession had broken up, men and women, young men and maidens came together to the same place. There they saw one another, and Anthia was captured by Habrocomes, while Habrocomes was overcome by Love. He kept gazing more and more steadily at the girl, and though he wished to tear himself from the sight he could not, for the god pressed hard upon him and held him fast.

3.2. Anthia too was in a sorry state, receiving with her eyes wide open the beauty of Habrocomes as it streamed into her, and now scorning what is fitting for maidens. She would say something so that Habrocomes might hear, and would bare what parts of her body she could, so that Habrocomes might see. He surrendered himself to the sight and was the captive of the god.

3.3. And then, when they had sacrificed, they departed in grief, blaming the swiftness of their parting; and wishing to look at one another, they kept turning round and lingering, and found many pretexts for delay.

3.4. But when each had gone home, then they realized into what evils they had fallen. The memory of the other's face came over them, and love was kindled within them, and through the rest of the day they fed their desire; and when they went to sleep they came all at once into their distress, and the love within each of them was beyond all checking.

4.1. So Habrocomes seized his hair and tore his clothes, and said, "Alas for my misery! What has happened to me, wretch that I am? I, Habrocomes, until now so manly, who scorned Love, who reviled the god, am now taken and conquered, and forced to be the slave of a girl; and now someone appears more beautiful than I, and I call Love a god.
4.2. O coward that I am in everything, and base! Will I not hold out now? Will I not remain noble? Will I not be more beautiful than Love?

4.3. He is a god who is nothing, and I must conquer him. The girl is beautiful—but what of it? To your eyes, Habrocomes, Anthia is shapely; yet, if you will it, she is not so to you. Let this be resolved: Love shall never master me."

4.4. So he spoke; but the god pressed upon him more violently, dragged him though he resisted, and tormented him against his will. At last, no longer able to hold out, he threw himself upon the ground and said, "You have conquered, Love; a great trophy has been raised over chaste Habrocomes.

4.5. You have a suppliant. Save the man who has fled to you, the lord of all. Do not overlook me, nor punish the rash one too long. I scorned your power, Love, because I was still without experience; but now give Anthia back to me. Be not only harsh to one who resisted, but a kindly god to one who has been overcome." So he spoke; but Love was still angry, and was minded to exact a great penalty from Habrocomes for his disdain.

4.6. Anthia too was in a sorry state, and no longer able to bear it she roused herself, trying to hide it from those present. "What," she said, "has happened to me, wretched as I am? A maiden in love beyond my years, I suffer strange torments, unfitting for a girl. I am mad for Habrocomes—beautiful, yes, but proud.

4.7. And what will be the limit of my desire, and what the end of my misery? My beloved is haughty, I am a guarded maiden. What helper shall I find? To whom shall I confide my troubles? Where shall I see Habrocomes?"

5.1. Thus each of them lamented all night long, and they held before their eyes the faces of one another, forming the images of each other in their souls. When day came, Habrocomes went off to his accustomed exercises, and the maiden to her habitual worship of the goddess.
5.2. Their bodies too were worn out from the night that had passed, their looks dejected, and their complexions changed; and this went on for a long time, and they made no further progress.

5.3. Meanwhile, spending their days in the temple of the goddess, they kept gazing at one another, ashamed and afraid before each other to tell the truth. Only this much: Habrocomes would sometimes groan and weep and pray piteously, while the girl listened;

5.4. and Anthia suffered the same, but was gripped by an even greater affliction. If ever she saw other maidens or women looking at him—and all of them looked at Habrocomes—it was plain that she was distressed, for she feared to be outshone. The prayers each of them made to the goddess were the same in substance, secret though they were, and they turned out alike.

5.5. As time went on, the youth could endure it no longer; his whole body had wasted away and his soul had collapsed, so that Lycomedes and Themisto fell into deep despondency, not knowing what was happening to Habrocomes, but alarmed by what they saw.

5.6. Megamedes and Euippe stood in like fear concerning Anthia, seeing her beauty withering while the cause of the affliction did not appear. At last they brought to Anthia seers and priests, in hope of finding a cure for the trouble.

5.7. These came and sacrificed victims, poured many kinds of libations, and uttered foreign words, saying that they were appeasing certain spirits, and they pretended that the affliction came from the gods of the underworld.

5.8. Lycomedes and his household also offered many sacrifices and prayers on Habrocomes' behalf; but no cure for the trouble came to either of the two—on the contrary, their love was kindled all the more.

5.9. So both of them lay sick, in a very dangerous state, expected at any moment to die, unable to declare their affliction. At last the fathers of both sent to a god's oracle to inquire the cause of the sickness and its release.

6.1. Not far off is the temple of Apollo at Colophon, a voyage of eighty stades from Ephesus. There the envoys of both households arrived and besought the god to give them a true oracle; and they had come on the same errand.
6.2. The god gave both of them one common oracle, in verse. The lines were these:

"Why do you long to learn the end of a sickness and its beginning?
One sickness holds them both, and from it the cure has arisen.
Dread sufferings I see for these two, and labours unending;
both shall flee over the sea, pursued by madness,
both shall endure bondage among men who mingle with the sea,
and a tomb shall be the bridal chamber for both, and destroying fire,
and beside the streams of the river Nile, to holy Isis
the saviour, you shall hereafter offer rich gifts.
But still, after their sufferings, a better fate awaits them."

7.1. When this oracle was brought to Ephesus, at once the fathers were at a loss, and were utterly at sea as to what the trouble was; for they could not interpret the words of the god—neither what the sickness was, nor the flight, nor the bonds, nor the tomb, nor the river, nor the help from the god.

7.2. So, after much deliberation, they decided to soften the oracle as best they could, and to join the children in marriage, since this too seemed to be the god's will from what he had prophesied. They resolved on this, and determined to send the pair abroad for a time after the marriage.

7.3. The city was already full of merrymakers, everything was garlanded, and the coming marriage was on every tongue; everyone counted them blessed—him, for the kind of wife he would take; her, for the kind of youth she would lie beside.

7.4. When Habrocomes learned both of the oracle and of the marriage, he rejoiced greatly that he would have Anthia, and the prophecies caused him no fear at all, but the present seemed to him sweeter than any terror. In the same way Anthia rejoiced that she would have Habrocomes; what the flight or the misfortunes might be she made light of, having in Habrocomes a consolation for all the evils to come.

8.1. So when the time for the marriage had come, all-night festivities were held and many victims sacrificed to the goddess. When these had been completed and night had come—though everything seemed slow to Habrocomes and Anthia—they led the girl to the bridal chamber with torches, singing the wedding hymn and shouting blessings; and bringing her in, they laid her down.

8.2. Their bridal chamber had been prepared in this way: a golden couch was spread with purple coverlets, and over the couch a Babylonian canopy was embroidered: Loves at play, some attending Aphrodite (for there was also an image of Aphrodite), some riding as mounted archers on sparrows, some weaving garlands, some carrying flowers—

8.3. these on one part of the canopy; and on the other was Ares, not in armour, but adorned as for his beloved Aphrodite, garlanded, wearing a mantle; and Love led him, holding a lighted torch. Beneath this very canopy they laid Anthia, having brought her to Habrocomes, and shut the doors.

9.1. The same feeling came over them both, and they could neither speak to one another nor look each other in the eyes, but lay overcome by pleasure, ashamed, afraid, and panting; their bodies throbbed and their souls trembled.

9.2. At last Habrocomes recovered himself and embraced Anthia; she wept, her desire sending forth her tears as tokens of her soul. And Habrocomes said, "O night most longed for by me, which I have at last won, after so many wretched nights before.

9.3. O girl sweeter to me than light, and more blessed than any of whom story has ever told—you have for your husband a man who loves you, with whom it will be granted to a chaste woman to live and die." So saying, he kissed her and caught her tears, and to him those tears seemed more refreshing than any nectar and more potent than any drug against pain.

9.4. She, with a few words to him, said, "So, Habrocomes, do I seem beautiful to you, and after your own loveliness do I please you? Coward and timid one, how long a time you delayed in your love! How long you held back! From my own sufferings I know what you have suffered.

9.5. But come, receive my tears, and let your beautiful hair drink the draught of love; and let us cling and mingle together, and drench our garlands with each other's tears, that these too may share our love."

9.6. So saying, she kissed his whole face, pressed all his hair to her eyes, took up the garlands, and joining lips to lips in kisses she fitted them together; and all that they thought passed from soul into the other's soul through the kiss.

9.7. And kissing his eyes she said, "O you who have often grieved me, who first planted the goad in my soul, you who were then so proud, now so full of love, well have you served me, and well have you led my love into the soul of Habrocomes.

9.8. Therefore I kiss you again and again, and I fit my own eyes to you, the servants of Habrocomes. May you always look upon him, and never show another beautiful woman to Habrocomes, nor let any other man seem shapely to me. You hold the souls that you yourselves have kindled; keep them safe as they are."

9.9. So she spoke; and clinging together they took their rest and enjoyed the first fruits of Aphrodite, and all night long they vied with each other, each striving to seem the one who loved the more.
10.1. When day came, they rose far happier and far more cheerful, having at last fairly enjoyed what they had so long desired.

10.2. Their whole life was a festival, everything was full of good cheer, and now there was even a forgetting of the prophecies. But destiny was not forgotten, nor did the god to whom these things were appointed neglect them.

10.3. After a little time had passed, the fathers decided to send them out of the city according to their plans; for the pair were to see another land and other cities, and so, as far as possible, to soften the oracle of the god by being away from Ephesus for a time.

10.4. So everything was made ready for their departure: a great ship and sailors ready to set sail, and the provisions were put aboard—abundant and varied clothing, much silver and gold, and an overflowing plenty of food.

10.5. Before the sailing there were sacrifices to Artemis, prayers from the whole people, and tears from all, as for children who belonged to them all and were about to depart. Their voyage had been arranged for Egypt.

10.6. When the day of departure came, there were many menservants and many maidservants; and as the ship was about to put out, the whole multitude of the Ephesians was there to escort them, and many of the . . . with torches and sacrifices.

10.7. Meanwhile Lycomedes and Themisto, with everything coming back to their minds at once—the oracle, their son, his going abroad—lay upon the ground in despondency. Megamedes and Euippe had felt the same, but were more cheerful, looking to the ends of the prophecies.
10.8. By now the sailors were busy, the stern-cables were being loosed, the helmsman was taking up his place, and the ship was beginning to move off.

10.9. There was a great and confused outcry from those on land and those on the ship, the one side saying, "O dearest children, shall we who begot you ever see you again?" and the others, "O fathers, shall we recover you?" There was weeping and wailing, and each called his own kin by name, leaving the name with one another as a remembrance.

10.10. Megamedes took a cup, poured a libation, and prayed so as to be heard by those on the ship, saying, "O children, may you above all be fortunate and escape the harsh prophecies, and may the Ephesians receive you home in safety, and may you recover your dearest fatherland. But if anything else should befall, know this, that we too shall live no longer; we send you forth on a road that is unhappy, but necessary."

11.1. As he was still speaking and going out, his tears checked his words. The crowd went off into the city, urging them to take courage; but Habrocomes and Anthia lay clinging to one another, thinking of many things at once—pitying their parents, longing for their fatherland, dreading the oracle, suspicious of the journey; yet the voyage in each other's company was a consolation to them in everything.

11.2. That day, with a favourable wind, they completed their voyage and put in at Samos, the holy island of Hera. There they sacrificed, made their meal, and with many prayers set sail again as night came on.

11.3. Their voyage was prosperous, and they talked much with one another: "Will it be granted to us to live out our lives together?" And once Habrocomes, with a great groan, fell to thinking of his own case and said, "Anthia, dearer to me than my own soul, may we above all be fortunate and come safe through together;

11.4. but if it is fated that we suffer something, and we are somehow parted from one another, let us swear to each other, dearest, that you will remain chaste for me and endure no other man, and that I, for my part, would never live with any other woman."

11.5. Hearing this, Anthia gave a great cry and said, "What is this, Habrocomes? Have you believed that, if I am parted from you, I will still think of a husband and marriage—I, who would not even live at all without you? I swear to you by the goddess of our fathers, the great Artemis of the Ephesians, and by this sea that we are crossing, and by the god who has so well driven us mad for one another, that even if I am torn from you for a little while, I will neither live nor look upon the sun."

11.6. So Anthia spoke; and Habrocomes swore the same in turn, and the moment made their oaths the more solemn. Meanwhile the ship passed by Cos and Cnidus, and the island of the Rhodians came into view, great and beautiful; and there they had to put in by all means, for the sailors said they must take on water and rest themselves, since they were about to enter on a long voyage.

12.1. So the ship put in at Rhodes, and the sailors disembarked; Habrocomes went out leading Anthia by the hand. All the Rhodians gathered, struck by the beauty of the young pair, and no one who saw them passed by in silence: some said it was a visitation of gods, others bowed down and worshipped. Soon the names of Habrocomes and Anthia had run through the whole city.

12.2. The people offered public prayers for them, sacrificed many victims, and kept their visit as a festival. The pair viewed the whole city, and dedicated in the temple of the Sun a suit of golden armour, with an inscription as a memorial of those who had dedicated it:

"These wrought-gold arms were set here for you as a gift,
by Anthia and Habrocomes, citizens of holy Ephesus."

12.3. Having made this dedication and stayed a few days on the island, they set sail again at the urging of the sailors, after taking on provisions; and the whole multitude of the Rhodians escorted them. At first they were carried along by a favourable wind, and the voyage was a pleasant one; that day and the following night they were carried on, traversing the sea called Egyptian. But on the second day the wind dropped, there was a calm, the voyage was slow, the sailors grew idle, and there was drinking and drunkenness—and the beginning of the prophecies.

12.4. Meanwhile a woman appeared to Habrocomes, terrible to look upon, greater than human in size, wearing a crimson robe. Standing over the ship, she seemed to set it on fire, and the others perished, but he, with Anthia, swam to safety. As soon as he saw this he was troubled, and expected some calamity from the dream; and the calamity came to pass.

13.1. There happened to be at Rhodes pirates lying in wait for them, Phoenicians by race, in a great trireme. They lay at anchor as men carrying cargo, and they were many and bold. These had learned that on the ship there was gold and silver and many slaves of great value.
13.2. So they resolved to fall upon them, kill those who resisted, and carry off the rest to Phoenicia to be sold, along with the goods; for they despised them as no match in a fight.
13.3. The leader of the pirates was called Corymbus, a young man great to look upon, terrible in his gaze; his hair was unkempt and hung loose.

13.4. When the pirates had laid these plans, at first they sailed quietly alongside Habrocomes and his company; but at last—it was about midday, and all those on the ship were lying about from drink and idleness, some asleep, some listless—Corymbus and his men bore down upon them, driving their ship with great speed.

13.5. When they came near, they leaped armed onto the ship, with their swords drawn. At that some flung themselves into the sea in terror and perished, while others, wishing to defend themselves, were cut down.

13.6. But Habrocomes and Anthia ran to Corymbus the pirate, and grasping his knees said, "Master, take the goods, and us too as your slaves, but spare our lives and kill no more of those who have willingly put themselves into your hands. By the sea itself, by your own right hand, lead us wherever you wish, and sell us as your slaves; only take pity on us, and put us under one master."

14.1. Hearing this, Corymbus at once ordered them to stop killing. He transferred the more valuable of the cargo, together with Habrocomes and Anthia and a few of the other servants, and set fire to the ship; all the rest were burned up, for he could neither carry them all off nor saw it safe to do so.
14.2. It was a pitiable spectacle: some being carried off in the trireme, others, in the burning ship, stretching out their hands and lamenting.

14.3. Some cried, "Where will you be taken, masters? What land will receive you, and what city will you live in?" Others said, "O blessed are you, who are about to die happily before you have known bonds, before you have seen the slavery of pirates." So they spoke, while some were carried off and others burned.

14.4. Meanwhile the tutor of Habrocomes, an old man now, venerable to look upon and pitiable for his age, unable to bear to see Habrocomes carried off, threw himself into the sea and swam as if to overtake the trireme, saying, "To whom do you leave me, child—the old man, your guardian?

14.5. Where are you going, Habrocomes? Kill me yourself, unhappy as I am, and bury me; for what is life to me without you?" So he spoke, and at last, despairing of ever seeing Habrocomes again, he gave himself to the waves and died.

14.6. This of all things was the most pitiable to Habrocomes; he stretched out his hands to the old man and begged the pirates to take him up. But they paid him no heed, and after completing their voyage in three days they put in at Tyre, a city of Phoenicia, where the pirates had their home.

14.7. They did not bring them into the city itself, but to a nearby estate belonging to a man who was chief of a band of brigands, Apsyrtus by name, whose servant Corymbus was, for hire and a share of the spoils. During the passage of the voyage, from seeing him so much each day, Corymbus fell in love with Habrocomes, a violent love, and his familiarity with the youth inflamed him all the more.

15.1. During the voyage it seemed impossible to win him over, for he saw how wretchedly he was disposed from despondency, and he saw too that he was in love with Anthia; and to force him seemed dangerous, for he feared the youth might do himself some harm.
15.2. But when they had put in at Tyre, Corymbus could endure it no longer. At first he tended Habrocomes, urged him to take heart, and showed him every care;

15.3. and Habrocomes thought that Corymbus took such care of him out of pity. Then Corymbus confided his love to one of his fellow pirates, Euxinus by name, and begged him to be his helper and to advise him by what means he might win the youth over.

15.4. Euxinus heard Corymbus' tale with pleasure, for he himself was wretchedly disposed toward Anthia and loved the girl with a violent love. He told Corymbus his own case as well, and advised him not to torment himself any longer but to get to work;

15.5. for it was, he said, very ignoble that, after running such risks and venturing so much, they should not enjoy in safety what they had won by their labours. "We shall be able," he said, "to receive them as a special gift from Apsyrtus."

15.6. By saying this he easily persuaded the man, who was in love. And so they agreed in like manner to make their pleas, each on the other's behalf, and to win over—Euxinus, Habrocomes, and Corymbus, Anthia.
16.1. Meanwhile the two lay dejected, expecting much, talking with one another, and constantly swearing to keep the agreements they had made.

16.2. Then Corymbus and Euxinus came to them and, saying that they wished to speak privately, led them apart by themselves—the one Anthia, the other Habrocomes. The souls of the pair trembled, and they suspected nothing good.

16.3. So Euxinus spoke to Habrocomes on Corymbus' behalf: "Young man, it is natural that you should bear your misfortune hard, having become a slave instead of a free man, and poor instead of prosperous. But you must reckon everything to fortune, and be content with the spirit that governs you, and love the masters you have come to.

16.4. For know that it is possible for you to recover both prosperity and freedom, if you are willing to obey your master Corymbus; for he loves you with a violent love, and is ready to make you master of all that is his. You will suffer no hardship by yielding, but will make your master more kindly disposed toward you.

16.5. Consider the state you are in: no helper, this a foreign land, your masters pirates, and no escape from punishment for anyone who scorns Corymbus. What need have you now of a wife and such concerns? What need of a beloved, at your age? Cast everything aside; you must look to your master alone, and obey when he commands."

16.6. Hearing this, Habrocomes at once was speechless and could find no answer; he wept and groaned, looking inward at the state into which he had come. And then he said to Euxinus, "Allow me, master, to deliberate a little, and I will answer you on everything you have said."

16.7. So Euxinus withdrew; and Corymbus had spoken to Anthia of Euxinus' love, the present necessity, and the need for her by all means to obey her masters. He promised much—a lawful marriage, money, and abundance, if she would yield. She gave him a like answer, asking for a little time to deliberate.

1.1. So that day they returned to the cave, and what little strength they had left they restored to themselves and to their horses; for Hippothous too had a horse hidden in the wood. The next day they passed by Cilicia and made their way toward Mazacus, a great and beautiful city of Cappadocia.

1.2. For from there Hippothous planned, by gathering young men in their prime, to form a robber band again. As they went through large villages there was abundance of all provisions, for Hippothous was skilled in the Cappadocian tongue, and everyone treated him as one of their own.
1.3. Completing the journey in ten days, they came to Mazacus, and there settled near the gates and decided to recover themselves for some days from their toil.
1.4. And as they were feasting, Hippothous groaned and shed tears; Habrocomes asked him the cause of his tears. He said, "My story is a long one, and full of tragedy."
1.5. Habrocomes begged him to tell it, promising to relate his own as well. So, taking it up from the beginning (for they happened to be alone), Hippothous told his story.

2.1. "I am," he said, "by birth from the city of Perinthus (the city is near Thrace), of those who are foremost in power there; and you have heard how famous Perinthus is, and how prosperous the men there.

2.2. While I was young I fell in love with a beautiful youth; the youth was one of the local people, and his name was Hyperanthes. I fell in love first when I saw him wrestling in the gymnasium, and I could not hold out.
2.3. So when a local festival was being held, and an all-night vigil at it, I went up to Hyperanthes and begged him to take pity on me. The youth heard me and, taking pity, promised everything.

2.4. The first stages of love were paved with kisses and touches and many tears from me; at last, finding our opportunity, we managed to be alone together, and our age put us above suspicion. And for a long time we were together, loving each other beyond measure, until some divinity grew jealous of us.
2.5. There came from Byzantium (and Byzantium is near Perinthus) a man among the foremost in power there, proud of his wealth and abundance; he was called Aristomachus.

2.6. As soon as he set foot in Perinthus, as if sent by some god against me, he saw Hyperanthes with me and was at once captivated, marvelling at the beauty of the youth—beauty that could draw anyone whatever.

2.7. Having fallen in love, he no longer kept his passion within bounds, but at first sent messages to the youth; and when that was impossible for him (for Hyperanthes, out of his affection for me, would let no one approach), he persuaded the youth's father, a base man and weaker than money.
2.8. His father gave him Hyperanthes on the pretext of teaching, for Aristomachus claimed to be a master of rhetoric. Taking him, he at first kept him shut up, and after this departed for Byzantium.

2.9. I followed too, despising all my own affairs, and I was with the youth as much as I could be; but I could do little, and a kiss became a rare thing for me, and talk difficult, for I was watched by many.

2.10. At last, no longer able to bear it, I goaded myself and went back to Perinthus, sold all the property I had, gathered the money, and came to Byzantium; and taking a small sword (this too seemed good to Hyperanthes), I went by night into the house of Aristomachus, found him lying with the boy, and, filled with rage, struck Aristomachus a mortal blow.

2.11. While all was quiet and everyone at rest, I went out unnoticed, just as I was, taking Hyperanthes with me; and travelling all night to Perinthus, I at once boarded a ship, with no one knowing, and sailed for Asia.

2.12. For a while the voyage went prosperously; but at last, when we were off Lesbos, a violent wind fell upon us and overturned the ship. I swam along with Hyperanthes, supporting him and making his swimming lighter; but when night came the youth could endure no longer, gave out in the swimming, and died.

2.13. I managed only to bring his body safe to land and to bury it. With many tears and groans, I gathered his remains, and finding somewhere a suitable stone, I set up a pillar over the tomb and inscribed on it, in memory of the unhappy youth, an epigram that I composed on the spot:

Hippothous made this tomb for renowned Hyperanthes,
no fitting grave from death for a holy citizen,
deep beneath the earth—a glorious flower, whom once a divinity
snatched away on the sea, while a great gale blew.

2.14. After that I resolved not to go to Perinthus, but turned through Asia toward Greater Phrygia and Pamphylia; and there, from want of a living and from despondency at my misfortune, I gave myself to a robber band. At first I became a servant of the band, but at last I myself organized a band around Cilicia, which was renowned for a long time, until my companions were taken not long before I saw you.
2.15. Such is the fortune of my story. But you, dearest, tell me your own; for it is clear that you too are under some great compulsion in your wandering."

3.1. So Habrocomes told that he was an Ephesian, that he had fallen in love with a girl and married her, and of the oracles, and the journey abroad, and the pirates, and Apsyrtus, and Manto, and the bonds, and the flight, and the goatherd, and the road as far as Cilicia.

3.2. While he was still speaking, Hippothous joined him in lamenting and said, "O my parents, O fatherland that I shall never see again, O Hyperanthes, dearest of all to me! You, Habrocomes, will at least see your beloved and recover her at last in time; but I can never see Hyperanthes again."
3.3. As he spoke he showed a lock of hair and wept over it. When both had lamented their fill, Hippothous, looking at Habrocomes, said, "There is another story I passed over without telling.

3.4. A little before the band was taken, a beautiful girl came wandering to the cave, of the same age as you, and she said your fatherland was hers; more than that I did not learn. It was decided to sacrifice her to Ares. Everything was made ready, when our pursuers came upon us; and I escaped, but what became of her I do not know.

3.5. She was very beautiful, Habrocomes, and plainly dressed; golden hair, charming eyes." While he was still speaking, Habrocomes cried out, "You have seen my Anthia, Hippothous! Where has she fled, then? What land holds her? Let us turn toward Cilicia, let us seek her; it is not far from the band.

3.6. Yes, by the very soul of Hyperanthes, do not willingly wrong me, but let us go where we can find Anthia." Hippothous promised to do everything, but said they must gather a few men for the safety of the road.

3.7. So they were occupied with this, planning how they should go back to Cilicia. Meanwhile, for Anthia the thirty days had passed, and the preparations for the marriage were being made by Perilaus: victims were brought down from the country, and there was great abundance of everything besides. With him were his household and kinsmen, and many of the citizens too came to celebrate Anthia's wedding.

4.1. During the time when Anthia, taken from the band, had come to Tarsus, there arrived an old Ephesian, a physician by profession, Eudoxus by name; he had come to Egypt after falling into a shipwreck on his voyage.

4.2. This Eudoxus went about to the other men too, all those of Tarsus most esteemed, asking from some clothing, from others money, and telling each his misfortune; and he came to Perilaus too and said that he was an Ephesian and a physician by profession.

4.3. Perilaus took him and led him to Anthia, thinking she would be pleased to see a man who was an Ephesian. She greeted Eudoxus kindly and inquired whether he could tell her anything about her own people; but he said he knew nothing, since his absence from Ephesus had been a long one. None the less, Anthia was glad of him, recalling her home.
4.4. So he became a familiar of the household and went in constantly to Anthia, enjoying all provisions, and always begging her to send him back to Ephesus; for he had children and a wife.

5.1. So when all the preparations for the wedding had been completed by Perilaus, and the day was at hand, a costly banquet had been made ready for him, and Anthia had been adorned in bridal array. But she ceased not to weep, neither by night nor by day, and always held Habrocomes before her eyes.

5.2. She thought of many things at once—her love, her oaths, her fatherland, her parents, the necessity, the marriage. And so, finding herself alone and seizing the moment, she tore her hair and said, "Wholly unjust and base am I, who do not repay Habrocomes in like measure.

5.3. For he, that he might remain my husband, endures bonds and tortures, and perhaps even has died; but I am forgetful of these things and am being married, wretch that I am, and someone will sing the wedding hymn over me, and I shall come to the bed of Perilaus.
5.4. But, dearest soul of Habrocomes, do not grieve at all on my account; for I would never willingly wrong you. I will come to you, and remain until death your bride."

5.5. So she spoke; and when Eudoxus the Ephesian physician came to her, she led him aside to a quiet room, fell at his knees, and begged him to tell no one anything of what she was about to say, and adjured him by the goddess of her fathers, Artemis, to help her in all that she should ask of him.

5.6. Eudoxus raised her up, for she was lamenting much, urged her to take heart, and swore, promising to do everything. So she told him of her love for Habrocomes, and the oaths to him, and the agreements about her chastity.

5.7. "If it were possible," she said, "for me, alive, to recover Habrocomes alive, or to escape and run away from here unnoticed, I would take counsel about these things. But since he is dead, and flight is impossible, and it is unbearable for me to endure the coming marriage—for I will neither break my agreements with Habrocomes nor disregard my oaths—do you, then, become my helper, finding somewhere a drug that will release me, ill-fated as I am, from my troubles.

5.8. And in return you will have many blessings from the gods, to whom I will pray for you often even before my death; and I myself will give you money and arrange your passage home. You will be able, before anyone learns of it, to board a ship and sail for Ephesus; and arriving there, seek out my parents Megamedes and Euippe, and tell them of my death and all that happened on the journey, and say that Habrocomes is dead."

5.9. So saying, she rolled at his feet and begged him to contradict her in nothing and to give her the drug. And bringing out twenty minas of silver and her necklaces (for she had all things in abundance, having control over all of Perilaus' goods), she gave them to Eudoxus. He, after much deliberation, pitying the girl for her misfortune, and longing for the road to Ephesus, and overcome by the silver and the gifts, promised to give the drug, and went off to fetch it.
5.10. Meanwhile she lamented much, bewailing her own youth and grieving that she was to die before her time, and called often upon Habrocomes as though he were present.

5.11. After a little while Eudoxus came, bringing not a deadly drug but a sleeping one, so that the girl should suffer no harm and he himself, having got his provisions for the journey, might come safe home. Anthia took it, gave him many thanks, and sent him away. And he at once boarded a ship and set sail, while she looked for a suitable moment to drink the drug.

6.1. By now it was night; the bridal chamber was being prepared, and those appointed to the task came to lead Anthia out. She went out unwilling and in tears, hiding the drug in her hand; and when she came near the chamber, the household raised the wedding hymn.
6.2. But she lamented and wept, saying, "Once before I was led like this, with Habrocomes for my bridegroom, and the fire of love escorted us, and the wedding hymn was sung over a happy marriage.

6.3. But now what will you do, Anthia? Will you wrong Habrocomes—your husband, your beloved, who has died for your sake? I am not so cowardly, nor so timid in my troubles. Let this be resolved: let us drink the drug. Habrocomes must be my only husband; him I desire, even dead."

6.4. So she spoke, and was led into the chamber. And when she was alone—for Perilaus was still feasting with his friends—she pretended that in her agitation she was seized by thirst, and ordered one of the servants to bring her water, as if to drink. When the cup was brought, she took it, and with no one present within, threw in the drug, and weeping said,

6.5. "O soul of dearest Habrocomes, behold, I fulfil my promises to you and come the road to you—an unhappy road, but a necessary one. Receive me gladly, and grant me there with you a happy life." So saying, she drank the drug; and at once sleep took hold of her, and she fell to the ground, and the drug did all that it could.

7.1. When Perilaus came in and at once saw Anthia lying there, he was struck with horror and cried out, and there was great confusion in the house and mingled emotions—wailing, fear, dismay. Some pitied her who seemed to have died, others grieved with Perilaus, and all lamented what had happened.

7.2. Perilaus rent his clothes, fell upon the body, and said, "O dearest girl, who before the marriage have left your lover, having for a few days been the bride of Perilaus—to what a chamber, the tomb, shall we lead you?

7.3. Happy, then, was that Habrocomes, whoever he was; blessed indeed was he, to receive such gifts from his beloved." So he lamented, and embraced her whole body, and kissed her hands and feet, calling her a wretched bride, an unhappier wife.

7.4. He adorned her, clothing her in rich garments and putting much gold about her; and no longer able to bear the sight, when day came he laid Anthia on a bier (and she lay senseless) and bore her to the tombs near the city. There he placed her in a chamber, sacrificing many victims and burning much clothing and other ornament.

8.1. So when he had performed the customary rites, he was led back to the city by his household. But Anthia, left behind in the tomb, came to herself and, realizing that the drug had not been deadly, groaned and wept and said, "O drug that deceived me, that hindered me from travelling the happy road to Habrocomes! I have failed, then, even of the desire for death—a new misfortune.

8.2. But it is still possible, by staying in the tomb, to accomplish the work of the drug through starvation. For no one would take me from here, nor would I look upon the sun nor come into the light." So saying, she held out, awaiting death nobly.

8.3. Meanwhile, when night had come, certain robbers, learning that a girl had been buried richly, and that much women's adornment lay buried with her, and much silver and gold, came to the tomb and, breaking open the doors, went in and were taking up the ornaments, when they saw Anthia alive. Thinking this too a great profit, they raised her up and wished to lead her away.
8.4. But she rolled at their feet and begged them much, saying, "Men, whoever you are, take all this adornment, whatever it is, and all that was buried with me, and carry it off; but spare my body.

8.5. I am dedicated to two gods, Love and Death; let me devote myself to them. By the very gods of your own fathers, do not bring out into the day one whose misfortune befits the night and the darkness." So she spoke; but she did not persuade the robbers. They led her out of the tomb, brought her down to the sea, put her aboard a small boat, and set sail for Alexandria; and during the voyage they tended her and urged her to take heart.
8.6. But she, thinking of the troubles into which she had fallen, lamenting and bewailing, said again, "Robbers and the sea, again I am a captive—but now more wretched, because not with Habrocomes.

8.7. What land, then, will receive me? What men shall I look upon? Not Moeris again, not Manto, not Perilaus, not Cilicia. May I come to a place where I shall see at least the tomb of Habrocomes." So she wept continually, and would take neither drink nor food, though the robbers forced her.

9.1. They, completing the voyage in a few days, put in at Alexandria, and there disembarked Anthia, and decided, when she had recovered from the voyage, to hand her over to some merchants. Perilaus, learning of the breaking-open of the tomb and the loss of the body, was in great and ungovernable grief.

9.2. Meanwhile Habrocomes kept searching and inquiring whether anyone knew of a foreign girl, a captive, brought from somewhere by robbers. When he found nothing, he gave up, worn out, and came to where they were lodging. Hippothous and his men had prepared a meal for them.
9.3. The others were dining, but Habrocomes was very despondent, and throwing himself on the couch he wept and lay there, taking nothing.

9.4. As the drinking went on, an old woman who was present among Hippothous' company, named Chrysion, opportunely began a story. "Listen," she said, "strangers, to a tragedy that happened not long ago in the city.

9.5. A certain Perilaus, one of the foremost in power, was elected to keep the peace in Cilicia; and going out in search of robbers, he captured and brought back some, and with them a beautiful girl, and persuaded her to marry him.

9.6. All the preparations for the marriage had been completed; but she, going into the chamber, whether driven mad or in love with someone else, drank a drug she had got from somewhere and died—for that was said to be the manner of her death." Hearing this, Hippothous said, "This is the girl whom Habrocomes seeks."

9.7. Habrocomes heard the story, but was overcome by despondency; at last, starting up at the sound of Hippothous' voice, he said, "But now Anthia is plainly dead, and perhaps her tomb is here, and her body is preserved."

9.8. So saying, he begged the old woman Chrysion to lead him to her tomb and show him the body. But she groaned and said, "This is the most wretched thing of all for the poor girl: for Perilaus buried her richly and adorned her; but robbers, learning what was buried with her, dug up the tomb, took up the ornaments, and made the body vanish. There is a great and mighty search for them by Perilaus."
10.1. Hearing this, Habrocomes rent his tunic and lamented greatly that Anthia had died honourably and chastely, but, after death, had perished wretchedly.
10.2. "What robber, then, is so amorous as to desire you even dead, and to carry off your body? I am robbed of you, wretch that I am, the one consolation left to me.

10.3. I am resolved, then, to die in any case; but first I will hold out until I find your body, and embracing it I will bury myself together with it." So he spoke, lamenting; and Hippothous and his men urged him to take heart.

10.4. And then they rested all that night; but thoughts of everything came over Habrocomes—of Anthia, of her death, of the tomb, of the loss of her body. No longer able to bear it, and unnoticed by all (for Hippothous and his men lay overcome with drink), he went out as if needing something, and leaving them all he came to the sea, found a ship setting sail for Alexandria, and embarked, hoping to overtake in Egypt the robbers who had carried off everything; an unhappy hope led him to this.

10.5. So he sailed toward Alexandria; and when day came, Hippothous and his men were vexed at Habrocomes' departure, but recovering themselves after a few days they decided to go robbing toward Syria and Phoenicia.
11.1. The robbers handed Anthia over to merchants in Alexandria, taking much silver; and the merchants fed her richly and tended her body, always seeking a buyer worthy of her.
11.2. There came to Alexandria a man from India, one of the kings there, to view the city and on business of trade, Psammis by name.
11.3. This Psammis saw Anthia with the merchants, and seeing her was captivated, and gave the merchants much silver and took her as his servant.

11.4. Having bought her, the barbarian man at once attempted to force her and use her for intercourse; but she, unwilling, at first resisted, and at last pretended to Psammis (barbarians are superstitious by nature) that her father had, at her birth, dedicated her to Isis until the time of her marriage, and she said the time was still set a year off.

11.5. "So if you outrage one consecrated to the goddess," she said, "she will be angry, and the punishment is grievous." Psammis was persuaded, did obeisance to the goddess, and kept away from Anthia; and she remained with Psammis under guard, regarded as sacred to Isis.
12.1. But the ship carrying Habrocomes missed the course to Alexandria and was cast ashore at the mouths of the Nile, at the place called Paraetonium and the part of Phoenicia along the sea.

12.2. As they were cast ashore, the herdsmen of that place ran upon them, plundered their cargo, bound the men, and led them by a long, desolate road to Pelusium, a city of Egypt, and there sold them off, one to one buyer, another to another. So Habrocomes was bought by an old soldier (he was discharged), Araxus by name.

12.3. This Araxus had a wife loathsome to look upon, much worse to hear, surpassing all in licentiousness, Cyno by name. This Cyno fell in love with Habrocomes as soon as he was brought into the house, and could no longer restrain herself; she was terrible both in falling in love and in wishing to gratify her desire.

12.4. Araxus was fond of Habrocomes and treated him as a son; but Cyno made a proposal of intercourse, begged him to consent, promised that he would have her for a wife, and that she would kill Araxus. This seemed dreadful to Habrocomes, and he considered many things at once—Anthia, his oaths, the chastity he had so often wronged already; at last, as Cyno pressed him, he consented.

12.5. And when night came, she, thinking to have Habrocomes for a husband, killed Araxus and told Habrocomes what she had done. But he, unable to bear the woman's wantonness, left the house and abandoned her, saying that he would never lie beside a murderess.

12.6. When she came to herself, at daybreak she went to where the crowd of the people of Pelusium was, lamented her husband, and said that the newly bought slave had killed him; and she made much lamentation and seemed to speak credibly to the crowd. They at once seized Habrocomes, and binding him sent him up to the man who was then governor of Egypt.
